n: Once Rehoboam felt secure and strong, he abandoned God’s law, and the people followed. Success and security often tempt people to forget God — a pattern the Book of Mormon calls the pride cycle.

f.w: he forsook the law of the LORD

n: In Rehoboam’s fifth year (about 925 BC), Shishak of Egypt invaded. The Chronicler states the spiritual cause plainly: they had been unfaithful to the Lord.

f.g: Pharaoh Shoshenq I, whose victory inscription at Karnak in Egypt lists towns in Israel and Judah.

n: Shishak came with 1,200 chariots, 60,000 horsemen, and countless troops, including Libyans, Sukkiim, and Ethiopians (Cushites).

f.g: Possibly a group of foreign troops serving Egypt; identity uncertain.
Cushites, from the upper Nile region (modern Sudan).

n: He captured Judah’s fortified cities — the very forts Rehoboam had built — and reached Jerusalem. Walls are no substitute for faith.
The prophet Shemaiah tells the king and leaders plainly: You abandoned Me, so I have abandoned you to Shishak.

f.w: Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you

n: The king and princes humble themselves and admit, “The LORD is righteous” — accepting that the punishment is just.
Because they humbled themselves, God spares them from destruction and grants partial deliverance. Humility immediately changes God’s response — a central theme in Chronicles.
Still, they will serve Shishak for a time, so they learn the difference between serving God and serving earthly kings.

f.w: that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms

n: Shishak carried off the treasures of the temple and palace, including Solomon’s famous gold shields. Within five years of Solomon’s death, much of his glory was gone.

f.w: the shields of gold which Solomon had made

n: Rehoboam replaced them with bronze shields — a sad picture of decline: bronze in place of gold, appearances maintained while true glory faded.
Whenever the king went to the temple, the guards carried out the bronze shields for ceremony and then returned them to the guardroom.

f.g: The armory of the royal guards.

n: Because he humbled himself, God’s anger turned away and Judah was not completely destroyed; some good things remained in the land.

f.g: Or ‘there were good things in Judah’ — some faithfulness remained.

n: Rehoboam regained strength and reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, God’s chosen city. He became king at forty-one; his mother Naamah was an Ammonite.

f.w: the city which the LORD had chosen

n: The summary of his reign: he did evil because he didn’t set his heart to seek the Lord. A heart not deliberately prepared for God drifts into sin.

f.w: he prepared not his heart to seek the LORD

n: Rehoboam’s deeds were recorded by the prophet Shemaiah and Iddo the seer. Fighting between Rehoboam and Jeroboam never stopped.
Rehoboam died and was buried in the City of David; his son Abijah succeeded him.
